title: Basic Problems of an Economy & Role of Price Mechanism
outcomes: State the central economic problem and its four basic problems with examples.
Explain the features of capitalist, socialist and mixed economies.
Explain how the price mechanism solves what, how and for whom to produce in a capitalist economy.
Evaluate the merits and demerits of each system.

meta.exam_tip: MCQs test the matching of features to systems (administered prices → socialism; consumer sovereignty → capitalism; joint sector → mixed). Learn three or four merits and demerits of each.

concepts.title: The central economic problem and its four parts
body: Every country — rich or poor, capitalist or socialist — has limited resources (natural resources, capital goods, consumer goods, money, time) with many alternative uses. Coal can run a factory, generate electricity or cook food; money can be spent in a thousand ways. If resources were unlimited, or if each had only one use, there would be no economic problem. The scarcity of resources relative to wants is called the central economic problem.

It splits into four basic problems: (1) What to produce, and how much of each? — more guns or more butter, more machines (capital goods) or more mobile phones (consumer goods), how many hospitals, schools, tonnes of wheat. (2) How to produce? — labour-intensive or capital-intensive techniques (handloom, power loom or automatic loom); the choice depends on the availability and relative prices of labour and capital, and society gains by using techniques that make best use of what it has. (3) For whom to produce? — how the output (the "national cake") is shared among people, i.e. distribution. (4) What provision for economic growth? — how much current consumption to give up for saving and investment so that productive capacity rises; with no provision, living standards stagnate and may later fall.

An economic system is the total set of arrangements and institutions through which a society produces and distributes goods and services — the mechanism that gives effect to its economic choices. Economies are grouped as capitalist, socialist and mixed according to ownership, mode of production and distribution, and the role of government.

blocks.title: Four basic problems

concepts.analogy: A family with one salary must decide what to buy, whether to cook at home or order in, how to share treats among children, and how much to save for the future — the four problems at home.
concepts.work: Government budgets, which CAs analyse every February, are a public answer to these four questions: what the state will produce, how, for whom and how much it will invest for growth.

concepts.title: Capitalist economy — features
body: In a capitalist (free market, laissez-faire) economy, factories, land, mines and other productive resources belong to private persons, who decide how to use them in order to earn profit. Private property is its foundation and the profit motive its driving force; the decisions of consumers and firms run the economy and, ideally, the government plays only a limited role. The USA, UK, Hong Kong and South Korea are often cited, though none is a pure form.

Features: (1) Right to private property — land, factories, mines can be privately owned, used as the owner likes and passed on by inheritance, subject to restrictions for public good. (2) Freedom of enterprise — anyone may start any business. (3) Freedom of economic choice — in consumption, work, production and exchange. (4) Profit motive — guides all activity. (5) Consumer sovereignty — the consumer is "king": buyers' spending decides what is produced and in what quantities. (6) Competition — the most important feature; it brings out efficiency. (7) Absence of government interference — no central plan; self-interest and the price mechanism run the economy automatically.
concepts.analogy: A capitalist economy is like a giant online marketplace with no central manager: sellers list what they think buyers want, prices rise for hot items and fall for unpopular ones, and production follows the money.
concepts.work: When CAs evaluate a start-up's business plan, they rely on capitalist features: freedom to enter, consumers' preferences shown through prices, and competition from rivals.

concepts.title: How the price mechanism solves the central problems
body: A capitalist economy has no planning authority, yet there is no chaos. The impersonal forces of demand and supply — the price mechanism (market mechanism) — coordinate millions of decisions.

What to produce: if consumers want more of a good, its price rises; with costs unchanged, profit rises and producers make more of it. If demand for a good falls, its price and profit fall and less is produced. Consumers "vote" with their spending. How to produce: each producer uses the technique that minimises cost — labour-intensive where labour is relatively cheap, capital-intensive where labour is relatively dear. Relative factor prices decide. For whom to produce: goods go to those with purchasing power, which depends on income — earnings from work, the prices of the factors one owns, and property owned. Consumption, saving and investment (growth): households consume and save, guided by income and the interest rate; entrepreneurs invest according to the expected rate of return on capital. Interest and the return on capital are the "prices" of capital.
concepts.analogy: Prices are traffic signals: a rising price is a green light telling producers "make more here"; a falling price is a red light saying "move your resources elsewhere".
concepts.work: Market research and pricing teams read these signals daily — a sustained price rise in a segment is a cue for capacity expansion, which CAs then evaluate through project appraisal.

concepts.title: Capitalism — merits and demerits
body: Merits: self-regulating through the price mechanism, with no cost of collecting information or running a planning machinery; private property and profit give strong incentives and efficiency; growth tends to be faster as investors choose only viable projects; resources go to their most productive uses; costs are minimised; consumers get variety and quality at reasonable prices and higher living standards; innovation and technological progress are rewarded; fundamental rights such as freedom and private property are preserved; enterprise and risk-taking are encouraged and the inefficient are penalised; it usually works within democracy.

Demerits: large inequality of income and wealth, dividing society into "haves" and "have-nots" and causing unrest; property rights placed above human rights; unequal opportunities; welfare ignored because the aim is profit; demand pattern reflects the purchasing power of the rich, not the real needs of society; exploitation of labour, strikes and job insecurity; consumer sovereignty often a myth; resources diverted to luxuries rather than wage goods; too few merit goods (education, health) and too many harmful but profitable goods; instability — overproduction, depression, unemployment; waste on advertising and sales promotion; growth of monopolies; excessive materialism and environmental damage.
concepts.analogy: Capitalism is a high-speed engine with weak brakes: it moves fast, but without regulation it can crash into inequality and instability.
concepts.work: Competition law, labour codes and environmental rules — areas where CAs advise on compliance — exist precisely to correct the demerits of an unregulated market.

concepts.title: Socialist economy — features, merits and demerits
body: The idea of socialism was set out by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in "The Communist Manifesto" (1848). The material means of production (factories, mines, capital) are owned by the community, represented by the State, and everyone shares the fruits on the basis of equal rights. It is also called a command economy or centrally planned economy, because a central planning authority allocates resources and market forces play little role. The central problems are solved through planning, aimed at maximum social welfare. The former USSR (1917–1990) is the classic example; China, Vietnam, Cuba and North Korea are also cited, though no country today is purely socialist.

Features: (1) Collective ownership of the means of production (small farms, workshops and trading firms may remain private); profit and self-interest are not the driving forces. (2) Economic planning by a central planning authority, which decides what, how much and how to produce. (3) Limited consumer choice — freedom from hunger is guaranteed but the range of goods is restricted; the right to work is guaranteed but choice of occupation is restricted. (4) Relatively equal distribution of income — little scope to accumulate private capital, and education and other facilities are shared more equally. (5) Minimum role of the price mechanism — prices are "administered prices" fixed by the planners; market prices play only a secondary role, such as clearing accumulated stocks. (6) Absence of competition — the State is the sole entrepreneur.

Merits: equitable distribution and equal opportunity (economic and social justice); rapid, balanced development through coordinated planning; better use of resources and no waste on advertising; minimal unemployment and stability without business cycles; a co-operative outlook instead of class war; right to work and a minimum living standard; protection of workers and consumers from exploitation; comprehensive social security.

Demerits: bureaucracy, delays, red tape, corruption and favouritism; loss of individual freedom; no right to private property; weak incentives to work hard; administered prices give no sound basis for cost calculation, so efficient allocation becomes impossible; state monopolies can become uncontrollable; limited consumer choice; no reward for personal efficiency; the extreme form is impractical.
concepts.analogy: A socialist economy is a school canteen run by the principal: everyone gets a fair, affordable meal, but the menu is fixed and the cook has little reason to improve the food.
concepts.work: Price controls and administered prices still exist in parts of mixed economies (for example, some essential drugs). Cost accountants and CAs are often asked to certify costs used to fix such prices — exactly the "basis for cost calculation" that socialism lacked.

concepts.title: Mixed economy — features, merits and demerits
body: A mixed economy relies on both markets and government to allocate resources; in fact every real-world economy is mixed to some degree. It tries to combine the best features of capitalism (private enterprise, profit motive, efficiency) and socialism (planning, welfare, equity) while avoiding the worst of each. The State runs important and strategic industries, allows private enterprise a positive role, and regulates the private sector so that it serves national welfare. India is a well-known example.

Feature — co-existence of private and public sectors, giving three sectors: (a) private sector — owned and managed by individuals and groups, driven by profit, but regulated by government policy; (b) public sector — set up by the State mainly for public welfare, not primarily for profit; (c) combined (joint) sector — government and private enterprise join hands to produce goods and services.

Merits: economic freedom and private property give incentives; price mechanism and competition push the private sector to efficiency; consumer sovereignty and choice; incentives for innovation, enterprise and risk-taking; benefits of planning and rapid development on plan priorities; greater equality and freedom from exploitation through state participation; harms of cut-throat competition checked by laws on environment and labour.

Demerits: a mixed economy is not always a "golden path". There may be excessive state control that cuts incentives and private growth, poor plan implementation, high taxes, inefficiency, corruption, waste, delays and poor public-sector performance; it is hard to keep the right balance between the two sectors; and without strong government initiative the private sector may grow out of proportion, so the economy drifts towards capitalism with its drawbacks.
concepts.analogy: A mixed economy is a road with both private cars and public buses, plus traffic police: freedom to drive, public transport for all, and rules to stop accidents.
concepts.work: CAs in India work across all three sectors — auditing private companies, public sector undertakings (often via C&AG-appointed audits) and joint-venture companies — a daily reminder of the mixed economy.

illustrations.title: How to produce: relative factor prices decide the technique
illustrations.q: A firm can produce 1,000 metres of cloth a day by Technique A (handloom: 40 workers + 2 machines) or Technique B (power loom: 10 workers + 6 machines). Machine cost is ₹3,000 per machine per day. (a) Which technique will a profit-seeking firm choose if the daily wage is ₹500? (b) What if the wage rises to ₹900? (c) Which basic problem does this illustrate, and how does a capitalist economy solve it?

solution.text: (a) At ₹500, A costs ₹26,000 and B costs ₹23,000. A is cheaper, so the firm chooses the labour-intensive technique.
(b) At ₹900, A costs ₹42,000 and B costs ₹27,000. Now B is cheaper, so the firm switches to the capital-intensive technique.

(c) This is the problem of "how to produce". In a capitalist economy, relative factor prices (the wage compared with the cost of capital) guide each firm to the least-cost technique, without any planner.

illustrations.title: What to produce: prices and profits as signals
illustrations.q: Two gadgets X and Y each cost ₹400 a unit to make and sell for ₹450; a firm sells 1,000 units of each. Consumers' tastes shift: the price of X rises to ₹520 and that of Y falls to ₹410. Compute the profit on each before and after, and explain how the market decides "what to produce".

solution.text: Profit on X rises from ₹50,000 to ₹1,20,000; on Y it falls from ₹50,000 to ₹10,000. Producers move resources from Y to X, so more X and less Y are produced — exactly what consumers asked for through their spending. This is consumer sovereignty working through the price mechanism.

jobs.title: Choosing between automation and manual packing
jobs.situation: Minimum wages in the state have gone up by 30%. Operations wants to buy automatic packing machines.
steps: Recognise the "how to produce" question: compare a labour-intensive and a capital-intensive technique.
Cost both methods per 1,000 units at the new wage, including machine depreciation, interest and maintenance.
Consider non-cost factors: flexibility, quality, social impact on workers, government incentives.
Recommend the least-cost technique, with a plan to redeploy workers.
jobs.takeaway: Relative factor prices change the best technique — the price mechanism at work inside a firm.
jobs.think: If the government gave a large subsidy on machinery, how would the decision change?
jobs.answer: The subsidy lowers the price of capital relative to labour, making the capital-intensive technique more attractive.

jobs.title: Advising a PSU on pricing
jobs.role: CA in a consultancy assignment for a public sector undertaking
jobs.situation: A state-owned fertiliser company sells at a government-fixed price below cost; the government reimburses the gap.
steps: Identify the administered price — a socialist tool used within India's mixed economy.
Compute the actual cost per tonne and the subsidy claim carefully, since there is no market price to guide efficiency.
Suggest cost-reduction measures, because without competition the incentive to cut costs is weak.
jobs.takeaway: Where prices are administered, cost data replaces the market as the guide — making accurate cost certification vital.

jobs.title: Joint-sector project appraisal
jobs.role: Articled assistant in a project finance team
jobs.situation: A state development corporation and a private company plan a joint venture for an industrial park.
steps: Note this is the combined (joint) sector of a mixed economy.
Map the objectives: the private partner seeks profit; the state partner seeks jobs and regional development.
Build the financial model so that both objectives are visible — returns for the private partner, employment for the state.
jobs.takeaway: Joint-sector projects must balance profit and public welfare — the essence of a mixed economy.

mcqs.explain: B costs 10 × 900 + 6 × 3,000 = ₹27,000, which is lower than A's ₹42,000.

questions.q: A shoe maker can make 500 pairs a day by Method P (60 workers + 4 machines) or Method Q (20 workers + 12 machines). Machine cost is ₹2,500 per machine per day. Find the least-cost method when the wage is (a) ₹400 and (b) ₹700 a day. Which basic economic problem does this solve, and by what mechanism in a market economy?

model.text: (a) At ₹400: P = ₹34,000, Q = ₹38,000 → choose P (labour-intensive). (b) At ₹700: P = ₹52,000, Q = ₹44,000 → choose Q (capital-intensive).
This is the "how to produce" problem; in a market economy it is solved by the price mechanism — relative factor prices lead firms to the least-cost technique.

scheme.pt: Names "how to produce" and price mechanism / relative factor prices

remarks: Good answers show both costs side by side before choosing.
mistakes: Comparing only labour cost and ignoring machine cost.
tips: Put both wages in one table — the switch in technique stands out.

questions.q: Explain with a numerical example how the price mechanism decides "what to produce" in a capitalist economy.

model.text: Suppose goods X and Y each cost ₹400 and sell at ₹450, giving a profit of ₹50 a unit. Consumers start preferring X: its price rises to ₹520 (profit ₹120 a unit), while Y's price falls to ₹410 (profit ₹10 a unit).

Higher profit attracts producers to X and lower profit pushes them out of Y. So more X and less Y is produced — the pattern consumers asked for through their spending. No planner is needed; prices act as signals. This is consumer sovereignty working through the price mechanism.

scheme.pt: Sets up a numerical example with costs and prices
Shows profit change following price change
Explains movement of resources towards the more profitable good
Links to consumer sovereignty / price mechanism

remarks: Examiners want the chain: demand → price → profit → output.
mistakes: Saying the government decides what to produce in capitalism.
tips: Write the chain with arrows before the example.

summary: Central problem = scarcity; four basic problems: what, how, for whom, provision for growth.
Capitalism: private property, profit motive, freedom of enterprise and choice, consumer sovereignty, competition, no government interference — solved by the price mechanism.
Socialism (Marx & Engels, 1848): collective ownership, central planning, limited consumer choice, relative equality, administered prices, no competition.
Mixed: co-existence of private, public and combined sectors; markets plus government.
remember: Price mechanism: demand → price → profit → output.
How to produce: decided by relative factor prices.
For whom: decided by purchasing power (income + property).
traps: The price mechanism is not absent in socialism; it has a secondary role.
Consumer sovereignty is a capitalist feature, but its reality is often called a "myth" in the demerits.
Mixed economy is not always a golden path — it has its own demerits.

cases.title: Rivertown chooses its economic system
cases.case: Rivertown is a newly independent island state. Its council is split. One group wants every factory and farm to be owned by the state, with a planning board deciding output and fixing prices. A second group wants no government role at all, with private owners free to produce whatever earns the most profit. A third group proposes that the state should run the port and power plant, private firms should run shops and factories under labour and pollution laws, and the state and a private shipping firm should jointly build a dry dock. The council also decides that 30% of national output should be saved and invested every year.

mcqs.q: The first group's proposal describes a:
mcqs.explain: State ownership, central planning and fixed prices are socialist features.

mcqs.q: Under the second group's proposal, what to produce would be decided mainly by:
mcqs.explain: In a free market, consumer demand and prices decide output.

mcqs.q: The dry dock built jointly by the state and a private shipping firm belongs to the:
mcqs.explain: Government and private enterprise joining hands = combined sector.

mcqs.q: If 30% of output is saved and invested, what percentage of output is left for current consumption?
mcqs.explain: 100 − 30 = 70% is left for current consumption. Deciding how much to save and invest is the basic problem of provision for economic growth.

mcqs.q: Labour and pollution laws for private firms are meant to correct which demerit of capitalism?
options: Exploitation of labour and environmental damage
mcqs.explain: Regulation checks the harms of unregulated profit-seeking.
